{{nihongo|'''Hanashiyama Shrine'''|羽梨山神社}} is a Shinto shrine located in Kamigo, Kasama City, Ibaraki Prefecture. The enshrined deity is Konohanasakuya-hime no Mikoto. It is a small shikinaisha of Hitachi Province, Ibaraki District, and its former shrine rank was village shrine. {{nihongo|'''Hanashiyama Shrine'''|羽梨山神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Hitachi Province]].

== History ==
In ancient times, the shrine was located halfway up Mount Hanashi.
In the 3rd year of Emperor Tenji (664), a small shrine dedicated to Konohanasakuya-hime no Mikoto was built on the mountainside of Mount Hanashi, which was rich in cherry blossoms, and this led to the shrine being called “Kashirayama Shrine.”<ref name="社伝">According to shrine tradition</ref>

In the 22nd year of Enryaku (803), Sakanoue no Tamuramaro prayed here for victory in his campaign to subjugate Mutsu and donated shrine buildings.<ref name="境内由緒石碑">From the shrine precincts history monument (July 29, 2019)</ref>

During the Jōhei–Tengyō Rebellion (the rebellion of Taira no Masakado), Taira no Sadamori dedicated bows, arrows, and gold dust and prayed here for victory in the subjugation of Taira no Masakado.<ref name="社伝">According to shrine tradition</ref>

In the Heian period, Minamoto no Yoriyoshi and Minamoto no Yoshiie dedicated spears, swords, armor, and sacred horses. Only the stirrups of the sacred horse still remain.
In the Kamakura period, Shishido Ienari, who moved from Kamakura, rebuilt the shrine buildings.<ref name="境内由緒石碑">From the shrine precincts history monument (July 29, 2019)</ref>

In the 11th year of Tenshō (1542), the shrine buildings on the mountainside of Mount Hanashi were destroyed by warfare, and the shrine was merged with Kumano Gongen at the mountain’s foothills, which became its current location. In the 8th year of Kanbun (1668), new shrine buildings were constructed.
In the 16th year of Genroku (1703), the current Myōjin-style stone torii gate was erected, and in the 4th year of Enkyō (1747), the current shrine buildings were constructed.
<ref name="境内由緒石碑">From the shrine precincts history monument (July 29, 2019)</ref>

During the Meiji period, due to the Shinto–Buddhist Separation Edicts, the shrine was separated from the administration of its former bettō-ji, the temple Fugen-in.

== Shrine rank ==
=== Divine rank ===
Hanishi-no-kami
* 12th year of Jōgan (870), August 23 – promoted to Junior Fifth Rank, Upper Grade<ref name="卷十八貞觀十二年">“Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku,” Volume 18, Jōgan 12 (870), August 28</ref>
* 1st year of Ninna (885), September 7 – promoted to Senior Fifth Rank, Lower Grade<ref name="卷四十八仁和元年">“Nihon Sandai Jitsuroku,” Volume 48, Ninna 1 (885), September 7</ref>

=== Modern shrine ranking system ===
Hanashiyama Shrine
* Meiji 6 (1868), April 1 – designated a village shrine<ref name="境内由緒石碑">From the shrine precincts history monument (July 29, 2019)</ref>
* Meiji 40 (1902), May 20 – designated as a shrine receiving offerings of sacred food and heihaku from the government<ref name="明治神社誌料">
“Meiji Jinja Shiryō: Prefectural and Village Shrines, Volume 1,” Ibaraki Prefecture section, Nishi-Ibaraki District, Village Shrines  
::Editor: Meiji Jinja Shiryō Compilation Office  
::Publisher: Meiji Jinja Shiryō Compilation Office  
::Publication date: Meiji 45 (1907)
</ref>

== Festivals ==
* New Year’s Festival (January 1)
* Setsubun Festival (February 3)
* Kinen Festival (April 11)
* Grand Annual Festival (second Saturday and Sunday of November)
* Niiname-sai (November 23)<ref name="境内由緒石碑">From the shrine precincts history monument (July 29, 2019)</ref>
